title: Mangrove Forests Are Growing Back Worldwide
paragraphs: Mangrove forests grow in salty water along tropical coasts, and they are valuable for several reasons. They protect the shore from erosion and storm surges, they give young fish and shrimp a safe place to grow, and they store up to four times as much carbon as taller tropical forests that grow inland.

For decades the news about mangroves was bad. A study published in the journal Science, led by Zhang from Tulane University, analysed satellite images taken between 1984 and 2023. It found that the area of mangroves fell by nearly 3,000 square kilometres between 1984 and 2010. After 2010, however, the area grew by nearly 2,000 square kilometres, especially in Asia, Australia and South America.

About two thirds of this growth came from mangroves colonising new ground, for example new mud on the coast, while about one third came from restoration of damaged forests. In Myanmar, the mangrove area dropped by 28.6 percent before 2010 and has risen by about 10 percent since. The picture is not the same everywhere, though: forests in the Niger Delta are still shrinking. The results also rely on satellite images, so local details may differ.

questions.q: How much carbon can mangroves store compared with taller inland tropical forests?
questions.a: Up to four times as much.

questions.q: What happened to mangrove area after 2010?
questions.a: It grew by nearly 2,000 square kilometres.
